question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8. After OLL, the top face is uniform, so PLL must be identified from the last-layer side stickers. Two adjacent side faces are not quite enough to disambiguate all rotated/mirrored PLL variants—especially cases like G- and R-perms where a hidden corner changes the exact case identity. You need the full three-sticker pattern on two adjacent faces plus the two corner stickers on a third side to fix the remaining ambiguity. That gives 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 non-top-facing stickers.

2.text:
In CFOP the U face is already oriented after OLL so the 9 U stickers carry
no permutation information.  The permutation of the last layer is carried
by the U-ring

* 4 U-corners : 1 U sticker + 2 side stickers each
* 4 U-edges : 1 U sticker + 1 side sticker each

i.e. 4×2 + 4×1 = 12 side stickers belong to the U layer.  On a conventional
hold you see the whole 12 sticker ring, the 4 edge side stickers and the
8 corner side stickers that sit round the U face.  In information terms
the ring is 8 pieces of information, 4 edges and 4 corners, so that with
the parity relation $p_{C}=p_{E}$ 7 independent non-U stickers are enough
to pin the 21 PLL classes down.  In ordinary practice the whole 12 sticker
U-ring, i.e. the 8 distinct U-pieces, is inspected, four edge side
stickers and four corner side stickers, the 12 stickers that are normally
quoted as the “side of the top layer”.

That is the 8 pieces / 12 stickers normally spoken of as the U-ring. The
12 stickers are 8 pieces of permutation information, 7 of them independent.
If the total number of side stickers that belong to the last layer is
counted it is the 12 side stickers of the U ring, 8 distinct pieces, 
commonly quoted as the 8 non-U stickers of information that have to be
read.

1.text:
In CFOP after OLL the U face is mono-chrome. The whole permutation
information of the last layer is therefore carried by the side colours
of the U layer.

The U layer consists of

* 4 U edges.  Each U edge is identified by its one side colour, the
U colour being the same for the four edges.
* 4 U corners.  Each U corner is identified by its two side colours,
the U colour being the same for the four corners.  

Hence in the whole cube there are

* 4 × 1 = 4 non-U stickers on the U edges,
* 4 × 2 = 8 non-U stickers on the U corners,

i.e. 12 distinct non-U stickers on the U layer.  Up to rotation you
can read the whole permutation on a single look.  In a normal
recognition position you read the four U edge side stickers and one
side sticker from each of the four U corners, 8 stickers that you can
see at once, which is the 8 distinct side colours of the U layer.
The eight distinct colours are the 12 distinct side stickers of the
U layer counted up to rotation, 4 edge side stickers plus 8 corner
side stickers in the absolute count.  This is the information that
distinguishes the 21 PLL permutations.

3.text:
In CFOP the U face is already colour solved after the OLL so that the whole
U-permutation is the only thing which is still unknown.  The U-layer is

* 4 U-edges, each of them is completely identified by its one side
colour, U–X ;
* 4 U-corners, each of them is completely identified by the unordered
pair of its two side colours, U–X–Y.

Hence up to a global rotation of the cube the PLL is the permutation of
the eight distinct U–layer pieces.  One sticker per piece is enough to
name the piece, i.e.

4 edges × 1 side sticker + 4 corners × 1 side sticker = 8

different side stickers, the 8th one being parity forced by the 4
edges + 4 corners.  In information theoretic terms the 8 pieces carry
only 7 independent colour choices and that is the usual “7 sticker’’
statement.

In the ordinary way of working the whole U-ring is inspected.  The
U-layer has 3 side stickers on each of the four side faces, 12
non-U stickers in all, 4 edge stickers + 8 corner stickers.  The 12
stickers are the 4×1+4×2 side stickers of the U-layer; once they are
known the permutation of the four U-edges and the permutation of the
four U-corners, i.e. the 21 PLL classes, is known.  The 8 piece
information is normally quoted as the 7 independent non-U stickers
which in practice is the whole 12 sticker U-ring. ∎

5.text:
In CFOP the OLL is finished before the PLL is started so that the whole
U face is mono-colour.  The U face itself therefore carries no
information at all about the permutation that is still left on the
last layer.  The information that is still missing is the identity of
the eight U-layer cubies

* 4 U-edges, each of which has one sticker which is not on U;
* 4 U-corners, each of which has two stickers which are not on U.

The U-layer therefore carries

$4\times 1+4\times2=12$

non-U stickers.  The eight cubies are distinguishable by the colour
that they show on the side faces.  Once you know the side colour that
a U-edge shows on the face on which it lies you know which edge is
there, and once you know one side colour of a U-corner you know which
corner is there up to the obvious rotation of the cube.  In the
conventional two-face view you are looking at the three stickers on
the top row of the front face and the three stickers on the top row
of the right face,

UF, UFL, UFR  and  UFR, UR, UBR,

i.e. the one identifying side sticker of each of the eight
U-layer cubies.  That is the eight distinct U-layer pieces, six
different physical stickers in a front-right view, that are normally
quoted as the ‘PLL recognition’ information.  If you want the whole
U-layer side information it is the twelve side stickers of the U
layer, four edge stickers and eight corner stickers, that are the
non-U information carried by the last layer.  This is the information
that is normally spoken of as the eight – in a practical two-face
view the six – non-U stickers that have to be read in order to tell
which of the 21 PLL classes you are in.  The twelve stickers are
$8$ distinct cubies and the usual working figure is the eight
identifying side stickers, six of which are visible at once on two
adjacent side faces. ∎

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is about what non-U information is actually needed after OLL in CFOP. All colleagues agree the U face is mono-colour after OLL so the U stickers carry no permutation information and the whole PLL is in the U-ring.

* The U-ring physically contains 4 U-edges ×1 side sticker + 4 U-corners ×2 side stickers = 12 non-U stickers, i.e. 4 edge side stickers and 8 corner side stickers. That is the 12-sticker side of the top layer that is normally quoted.
* Piece identification. An U-edge is named by its single side colour, 1 sticker per edge. An U-corner is named by the unordered pair of its two side colours; one side colour per corner is enough to name the piece up to global rotation, so one identifying sticker per piece is sufficient in practice. That is 4+4 = 8 distinct identifying side stickers, the usual “8 pieces” description of PLL recognition. The 12 physical side stickers are therefore 8 pieces of permutation information.
* Independence / parity. The 8 pieces satisfy p_C = p_E, so only 7 of the 8 identifying stickers are independent informationally. Several colleagues call this the 7-sticker information-theoretic minimum for the 21 PLL classes. Colleague 2 and 3 explicitly make the 7 independent / 8 piece distinction.
* Practical visibility. On a conventional hold you can see the whole 12-sticker ring by rotating the cube, and you can see the 8 identifying stickers at once. On two adjacent side faces you see the top row of each face: 3 stickers per face, 6 physical stickers, which correspond to the 1 identifying sticker per edge and per corner for the six U-pieces that lie on front/right. Colleague 4 formalises this as 3+3+2 = 8 non-top stickers needed to remove the remaining rotational/mirror ambiguity, e.g. for G- and R-perms.
* Disagreement is terminological: 12 = total non-U stickers belonging to the U layer; 8 = one identifying sticker per U piece, the number normally spoken of as “the PLL recognition stickers”; 7 = independent pieces after parity. No colleague disputes the 12-sticker total, the debate is whether the question asks for total physical stickers on the layer, the minimal sufficient identifying set, or the independent information count.

Unresolved for me: whether the question wants the physical count 12, the practical sufficient count 8, or the information-theoretic minimum 7. The consensus practical figure in the room is 8 identifying non-U stickers, with 12 physical side stickers on the U layer and 7 independent degrees of freedom.

4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4
4 U-corners × 2 side stickers = 8
i.e. 12 non-U stickers belonging to the last layer. The eight U-layer cubies are the 4 edges + 4 corners that have to be distinguished for PLL.

* Counting vs identification. 
1,2,3,5 stress the 12-sticker U-ring as the physical information content, 4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers. Up to a global rotation the permutation can be read from one side sticker per cubie, i.e. 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 identifying stickers. Because edge permutation and corner permutation have the same parity the 8 piece identifiers are only 7 independent in information-theoretic terms, the usual “7 independent non-U sticker” statement. 
1 explicitly says in a normal recognition position you can read four U edge side stickers and one side sticker from each of the four U corners, 8 stickers that can be seen at once.
5 nuances the practical view: in a conventional two-face view you see the three top-row stickers on front and the three top-row stickers on right, i.e. six physical stickers that identify the eight distinct U-layer pieces, six of which are visible at once, the whole U-ring being 12 stickers.

* Disagreement on minimum visibility. Colleague 4 argues a minimum of 8 non-top-facing stickers is required in practice, 3+3+2 across three faces, because two adjacent faces are not enough to disambiguate rotated/mirrored variants, e.g. G- and R-perms where a hidden corner changes the case identity. This is the 8-identifying-sticker claim made more concretely as a three-face inspection.

* Remaining tension. One side sticker per corner is not enough to name a corner by its unordered pair of side colours alone; a corner is defined by its two side colours. That is why the physical U-ring is 12 stickers. The 8-sticker identification relies on the spatial adjacency of the stickers and on the fact that the edge colours already anchor the colour scheme, so that in practice one side colour per corner together with the four edge side colours is sufficient to resolve the 21 PLL classes up to rotation. The information bound is 7 independent stickers, the operational teaching figure is 8 identifying stickers, and the physical count of non-U stickers on the U-layer is 12.

I am keeping the 12 physical non-U stickers on the U-layer, 8 distinct cubie identifiers, 7 independent in information theory, as the working picture, with the practical minimum visibility being about 8 stickers, typically realised as the 12-sticker U-ring inspected across at least three faces. The exact “must be seen” number is still contested between the 12-sticker physical total, the 8-sticker identifying set and the 7-sticker information bound.
